Classical Studies | Years 12–13 | October 2026   Page 1

About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Classical Studies Years 12–13 of the
New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Classical Studies Years 12–13 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Classical Studies Years 12–13 is proposed to
be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under
section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Classical Studies Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in Year 12
from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  In Classical Studies, students are taught multi-disciplinary methodologies about            Classical Studies leads to pathways in Classical Studies and related disciplines,
  Classical Greece and Rome, including social and political structures such as                such as humanities, history, philosophy, archaeology, and law.
  hierarchy and roles, cultural ideals such as excellence and duty, and cultural
  achievements. Students are taught how to examine literature, mythology, religion,
  art, archaeology, history, social life, and politics. They are also taught
  to recognise how these have been shaped and have shaped the foundations of
  Western civilisation, influencing art, literature, and society, and culture.

Students are taught to examine classical texts, material culture, belief systems, and
historical evidence to understand the ideas, values, and power structures that shaped
Classical Greece and Rome. They are taught to recognise and analyse how classical
societies have shaped and continue to influence cultures, institutions, and ways of
thinking across time and place.

Classical Studies provides students with the knowledge and practices to analyse
literature, art and architecture, and societies of Classical Greece and Rome; examine
classical primary sources as culturally situated artefacts; analyse evidence and
perspectives within broader social, political, and ideological contexts; apply core
disciplinary concepts, and develop critical and relational understandings of past
societies, including the transmission and influence of classical ideas across time,
place, and cultures.

As students progress through Years 12–13, they are taught to interrogate primary
evidence; evaluate competing interpretations of the classical world; synthesise
evidence, contexts, and viewpoints; and construct increasingly sophisticated
evidence-based interpretations, arguments, and judgements. This enables students
to develop informed and critical understandings of the classical world, engage
thoughtfully with multiple perspectives and knowledge systems, and draw well-
reasoned and defensible conclusions about how evidence, interpretation, and context
shape understandings of the past.

 Disciplinary writing

 Focus: The use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.
 In Classical Studies, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to explain, analyse, synthesise, evaluate, and justify interpretations of classical texts, material culture, ideas,
 and historical contexts for specific purposes and audiences.

Working with contexts
In Classical Studies, learning is organised and understood through contexts. These
are foundational sites of knowledge through which students encounter classical ideas,
practices, values, and ways of thinking in depth.
The tables below outline core contexts for Classical Studies in Years 12 and 13.
These contexts have been selected because they represent foundational areas of the
discipline and provide opportunities for students to develop and demonstrate the
specified knowledge and practices across the strands. Within each context, teachers
should choose topics that provide sufficient scope and complexity to support the
teaching sequence, drawing on material evidence to enable sustained interpretation,
comparison, and evaluation.
The Supporting Guidance provides examples of appropriate topic selection within
each context.

Death of Roman Republic (133 BCE–31 BCE)
   Caesar’s rise to power and death could be connected to its connection to and
    breaking of Republican politics, the shifting dynamics of political groups and their
    competing demands, and his interrelationship with key political rivals. This would
    include examining the background context of the Roman Republic, including the
    Gracchi, Marius and Sulla, and populares or optimates politics as it played out
    within the Republican political system. It would then include an examination of
    Caesar and key events that reflected his interrelationship with political factions
    and individuals. Finally, it would justify the significance by looking at the lasting
    impact of the power vacuum in the wake of his death and ultimately the rise of
    power of Augustus through the third civil war.

Interrelationship of classical knowledges
contexts
This strand should be embedded authentically within the study of art, literature, and
history or society, rather than taught as a separate component. Each topic or case
study should incorporate an authentic comparative or interpretive lens that connects
classical material to other knowledge systems, time periods, or perspectives.
Below are examples of what could be covered:
Connections
 Cross-cultural comparison: leadership, honour, gender roles, justice, warfare,
  hospitality
 Literature and storytelling: myth alongside other narrative traditions,
  reinterpretations in later texts
 Historical and social systems: law, governance, citizenship, empire
 Later receptions: Renaissance art, modern film, political rhetoric, popular culture
 Interpretive lenses: feminist, postcolonial, political, ideological readings.
Connections in mythology
 Rich cosmogonies with personified primal beings and genealogies of gods and
  humans (Gaia and Ouranos vs Ranginui or Papatūānuku and their descendants).
 Hero myths: Maui, Anansi, folklore heroes.
Connections in literature
 Middle Ages: Dante’s Inferno, Umberto Eco
 Renaissance: Shakespeare, Marlow, Milton
 Contemporary: Penelopiad, Percy Jackson series.
Influences in film
 Hero’s Journey template, Nolan’s Odyssey, Wolfgang Peterson’s Troy, depictions
  of Hercules.
Influences in art
 Medusa in Renaissance or early modern art (Cellini, Rubens, Bernini, Caravaggio,
  Verrocchio), Medusa in 19th to 21st century art (Victorian cameos, French or Italian
  19th century jewellery) and contemporary society (Garbatti, Hirst, PichiAvo, Moore,
  Versace)
 Architectural influences: Colosseum and modern arenas (Hnry stadium), Triumphal
  Arches (Arc de Triomphe).
